summary: Proposes two extensions to the Domain Name System. One is a method for storing and looking up records that map between network names and numbers, which is a proposed standard. The other is a set of ideas for describing mappings between arbitrary identifiers and numbers.

plainLanguage.summary: The Internet phone book normally maps computer names to numbers. This adds entries for whole networks too, so a network can be looked up by name.

questions: how to map network names to numbers in dns
how to find network name from ip address
subtitle: DNS extension for looking up networks by name and for general identifier-to-number mappings.

tldr.problem: The DNS can map host names to IP addresses, but cannot map network names to network numbers, which is useful for debugging and status displays. There is also a general need to map other types of identifiers to numbers.
tldr.mechanism: Use DNS to store network-to-address mappings by putting PTR records at host-zero addresses in the IN-ADDR.ARPA tree, and create a general framework called Yellow Pages (YP) for arbitrary identifier-to-number mappings using domain tree structure.
tldr.outcome: Networks can be queried by name in DNS alongside hosts. The Yellow Pages framework provides a pattern for future DNS extensions for TCP ports, protocols, autonomous systems, and other mappings.

facts.label: Class support
facts.value: Classes A, B, and C defined

today: RFC 1101 proposed extensions that remain largely experimental. While the basic mechanism for network name storage in DNS is sound, widespread adoption has been limited. Modern network management tools often use other mechanisms (SNMP MIBs, IPAM systems) to track network names and metadata. The Yellow Pages concept influenced later DNS extension patterns and the thinking behind service records and other DNS applications, but a global Yellow Pages was never fully implemented. The RFC remains available as a reference for organizations implementing network naming schemes in DNS.

sections.title: Why DNS Needs Network Names
sections.content: The Domain Name System maps host names to IP addresses, but it cannot map network names to network numbers. This capability existed in the old HOSTS.TXT file and is useful for debugging tools and status displays. The challenge in adding network name support to DNS is balancing two concerns: maintaining backward compatibility with existing host name support (which uses IN-ADDR.ARPA for address-to-name mappings) and creating a method general enough to serve as a precedent for future mappings, such as TCP port names to numbers or autonomous system names to numbers. This RFC proposes both a specific solution for network names and a general framework called Yellow Pages.
sections.plainLanguage: When you see an error message with a network number, it would help to know what network that is. This RFC explains how to look up network names in DNS just like you look up computer names.

sections.title: Network Name Syntax and Control
sections.content: Network names follow the same expanded syntax as modern host names, allowing leading digits as long as they do not conflict with IP address decimal notation. Unlike the old flat namespace for network names, the new approach integrates with the hierarchical DNS, allowing organizations to define their own network names under domains they control. For example, a network might be named isi-net.isi.edu or arpanet.arpa, depending on who owns it. This gives organizations local control while avoiding a centrally managed flat namespace that would become a bottleneck.
sections.plainLanguage: A network name is like a computer name: it can be nested in domains, like how you can have mail.google.com and maps.google.com for different services at Google.

sections.title: Storing Network Names in DNS
sections.content: Network-to-address mappings are stored in three places. First, at host-zero addresses in IN-ADDR.ARPA (e.g., 0.0.0.10.IN-ADDR.ARPA for class A network 10), using PTR records pointing to the network name and optionally A records containing subnet masks. Second, at the network name itself (e.g., isi-net.isi.edu), using PTR records pointing back to the host-zero IN-ADDR.ARPA entry. Third, at organization names (e.g., ISI.EDU), using PTR records pointing to their networks' host-zero IN-ADDR.ARPA entries. This three-way structure supports lookups in both directions and allows organizations to advertise their networks.
sections.plainLanguage: The phone book entries point in both directions: the network number points to the name, and the name points back to the number. Organizations can also list their networks.

sections.title: Looking Up Networks and Subnets
sections.content: To find a network name from an IP address, mask the address to the network boundary (class A, B, or C), construct the reversed host-zero IN-ADDR.ARPA name, and query for the PTR record. For example, 10.0.0.51 becomes a class A address, masked to 10.0.0.0, then reversed to 0.0.0.10.IN-ADDR.ARPA for the query. To find all subnets of an IP address, repeat the lookup for each subnet level using address masks from A records at each level. This extends the simple procedure to handle nested subnetting. Most organizations will use the DNS to resolve domain names to IP addresses and local tables to resolve port names to numbers, keeping the mappings simple.
sections.plainLanguage: To find a network's name, you reverse the network number to look it up in the phone book, just like looking up a phone number to find the person's name.

sections.title: Yellow Pages for General Mappings
sections.content: Beyond network names, many other mappings would benefit from DNS support: TCP port names to port numbers, protocol names to protocol numbers, autonomous system names to AS numbers, and Ethernet type names to type numbers. The RFC proposes a Yellow Pages (YP) framework, a precomputed index stored in a domain tree. Each YP uses a structure with a well-known origin (like IN-ADDR.ARPA), a from-data-type (the input), and a to-data-type (the output), creating domain names like 23.Number.TCP-port.YP. for port 23. Organizations can implement both centrally-managed YPs (for assigned network numbers) and organization-specific YPs (for local TCP ports). This framework establishes a pattern for future DNS extensions without requiring a new protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: The network name approach shows how to turn numbers into names in DNS. You can use the same idea for looking up anything else that has both a name and a number: ports, protocols, or types.
